findings.fact: D3 legally follows diamonds, and South can win with either diamond honor before developing clubs.
findings.explanation: North holds D3; South holds DA, DK and five clubs headed by CA and CK, opposite CQ. Clubs provide a feasible source of the additional tricks needed alongside the diamond and major-suit winners, with HK available as a dummy entry.
quotes: South has DA and DK to control diamonds, so dummy should conserve the higher spot card and play D3 under West’s DQ.
Win the diamond lead with DA or DK in hand, then use the club honors and established club tricks as the main source of tricks.

findings.fact: DK wins the current trick and implements the retained plan.
findings.explanation: The current trick is DQ–D3–D4, and South holds DK and DA. Playing DK wins while leaving DA as a later entry; the planned club development remains available.
quotes: West’s DQ is still winning, and South has both top diamonds. Use the lower winner, DK, preserving DA to regain the lead later.

findings.fact: Leading CK is a feasible start to developing South’s five-card club suit.
findings.explanation: South retains CA, CK, C8, C6 and C4 opposite CQ, C7 and C2. CK can win while dummy follows low; CQ and CA can subsequently help establish the remaining clubs. The plan makes establishment conditional and calls for reassessment.
quotes: Lead a club honor toward dummy’s CQ to establish club tricks while retaining CA as an entry and control.
Reassess after the defenders’ club plays.

findings.fact: Playing C2 preserves CQ without sacrificing the winning CK.
findings.explanation: South has led CK, West has followed C3, and North holds CQ, C7 and C2. CA is in South, so no defender can beat CK. Preserving CQ supports the continuing club-development route.
quotes: West followed low to CK, so dummy should play low and preserve CQ as a potential later winner.

findings.fact: The installed plan requires South to play CA after already leading C8 to the same trick.
findings.explanation: South leads C8, West plays second, North third and East fourth. If West covers C8, North can play CQ, but South cannot then play its CA: South has already played to that trick.
quotes: Continue clubs by leading C8 toward dummy’s CQ; if West covers, win with CA, otherwise let CQ take the trick.

findings.fact: CQ wins over C9, and the replacement plan retains available club resources and entries.
findings.explanation: North holds CQ over West’s C9; the only higher unplayed club is South’s CA. South also retains C6, C4 and DA, while dummy retains C7, allowing further club development and a return to South.
quotes: West’s C9 beats South’s C8, so use dummy’s CQ to win this trick rather than let the defense take it.
Win with CQ, then reassess the club position.

findings.fact: The reason asserts that East has a remaining club, although its location is unknown.
findings.explanation: East has played C5 and CT, and West has played C3 and C9. CJ is the sole outstanding defensive club and could belong to either defender. The stated purpose of drawing East’s remaining club assumes an unavailable holding.
quotes: lead C7 now to draw out East’s remaining club and keep control with CA.

findings.fact: C4 cannot take a trick currently headed by dummy’s C7.
findings.explanation: North led C7 and East discarded H2. South’s C4 ranks below C7, and West still has to play. Moreover, East’s discard establishes that West holds the outstanding CJ. Playing C4 therefore lets West win rather than taking the trick as the reason and installed plan claim.
quotes: East discarded on dummy’s C7, so South should take the trick cheaply with C4 and preserve CA as a control.
Take the club trick with C4, keeping CA and C6 for later control.
